court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: Where a tenant merely rented three rooms in the rear of a house and reached them via an outside stairway and landing, the letting did not include the stairway and landing; the landlord retained control of those areas and owed a legal duty (independent of contract) to keep them in reasonable repair, so a visitor injured by their collapse stated a valid negligence claim.

quotes.text: He said he had three rooms in the rear house, access to which was through a passageway from the street and by an outside stairway and along the landing to the door. Upon payment of the rent he gave her a receipt to show to the janitress who, he said, would give her the key.

This evidence did not show a hiring of the yard adjacent to the house, and the stairway and the landing together with the rooms, but only a hiring of the rooms themselves. This being so it followed that the landlord retained control of the stairway and landing.
Having retained such control it became her duty to exercise reasonable care to keep the stairway and landing in suitable repair for use.

notes: Letting of rooms in a rear tenement building treated as an ordinary lease of rooms only, with landlord retaining and duty-bound over common stairway/landing; who_was_letting classified commercial_operator because defendant owned a multi-building tenement property and acted through an agent, with no indication of owner-occupancy; duration of the tenancy itself is not stated in the opinion.
